lessons.title: Using the IDE & print()
lessons.summary: Writing your first line of code and displaying output on the screen.
lessons.notes:
The **IDE** (the code editor here) is where you write Python code. Type your code in the editor, then click **Run** to see what happens in the **Console** — the output panel where your program's results appear.

The simplest thing a program can do is display something on the screen, using the **print()** function:

```
print("Hello, world!")
```

Text goes in **quotes** (either "double" or 'single') — this tells Python "this is just text, not code to run". A number doesn't need quotes:

```
print(7)
```

Each print() starts a new line of output. To display more than one thing, use more than one print():

```
print("Line one")
print("Line two")
```

If you forget the quotes around text, Python tries to read it as code instead of text, and the program crashes with an error — `print(hello)` looks for something called `hello` that doesn't exist, rather than printing the word "hello".
lessons.worked_example:
print("Hello, world!")
print("This is my first Python program.")
print(42)
lessons.worked_example_note: Each print() call adds one new line to the output. "Hello, world!" needs quotes because it's text; 42 doesn't, because it's a number.

lessons.title: Getting input from the user
lessons.summary: input() lets your program ask a question and wait for an answer.
lessons.notes:
**input()** lets your program ask the user to type something while it's running. When Python reaches `input()`, the program pauses and waits — the user types an answer and presses Enter, and whatever they typed comes back as the result.

The simplest way to use it is to print it straight away:

```
print(input())
```

This just echoes back whatever the user typed. To use the answer more than once, give it a name so you can look it up again later:

```
name = input()
print(name)
```

The `=` here means "store whatever input() gives back under the name `name`" — you'll cover exactly what's going on with this properly in the next topic. For now, just know the pattern: get an answer with input(), store it under a name, then print that name whenever you want to show it.

You can print a question first, so the user knows what to type:

```
print("What's your name?")
name = input()
print(name)
```
lessons.worked_example:
print("What's your name?")
name = input()
print(name)
lessons.worked_example_note: The program pauses at input() until the user types something and presses Enter. Whatever they typed is stored under name, so print(name) can show it.

lessons.title: Concatenation — joining text together
lessons.summary: Using + to glue pieces of text into one.
lessons.notes:
**Concatenation** means joining pieces of text together. In Python, the `+` symbol does this for strings:

```
print("Py" + "thon")
```

This prints `Python` — the two pieces are glued together with nothing extra added. If you want a space between them, you have to add it yourself:

```
print("Hello" + " " + "World")
```

This prints `Hello World`, not `HelloWorld`.

Concatenation is useful for combining fixed text with something the user typed:

```
name = input()
print("Hello, " + name)
```

**Careful:** `+` only works when both sides are text (strings). Joining text and a number directly, like `"Score: " + 7`, causes an error — you'll cover how to fix that properly (casting) in the next topic.
lessons.worked_example_note: "Hello, " already has a space and comma built in, so + just glues name straight on the end with nothing extra added.

quiz.question: Which function displays text on the screen in Python?
quiz.explanation: print() is Python's function for displaying output on the screen.

quiz.question: Which of these will run without an error?
quiz.explanation: Text must be inside matching quotes. Without quotes, Python looks for something called hello, which doesn't exist, and the program crashes.

quiz.question:
How many lines of output does this produce?

print("A")
print("B")
quiz.explanation: Each print() call adds one new line of output, so two print() calls produce two lines.

quiz.question: What does input() do?
options: Pauses the program and waits for the user to type something
quiz.answer: Pauses the program and waits for the user to type something
quiz.explanation: input() pauses the program until the user types an answer and presses Enter.

quiz.question: After answer = input(), how do you display what the user typed?
quiz.explanation: The user's answer is stored under the name answer, so print(answer) shows it.

quiz.question: Which line correctly stores what the user types under the name reply?
quiz.explanation: = stores the value on the right under the name on the left. == compares two things instead of storing anything, so it wouldn't work here.

quiz.question: What does "Py" + "thon" evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: + joins the two strings directly with nothing in between.

quiz.question: Why doesn't "Hello" + "World" print Hello World with a space in the middle?
options: + doesn't add spaces automatically — you have to include one yourself
quiz.answer: + doesn't add spaces automatically — you have to include one yourself
quiz.explanation: Concatenation glues the two strings exactly as they are — any spacing or punctuation has to already be part of one of them.

quiz.question: What's wrong with "Score: " + 7?
options: You can't join text and a number directly with + — it causes an error
quiz.answer: You can't join text and a number directly with + — it causes an error
quiz.explanation: + only works when both sides are strings. Joining text and a number needs casting first — covered in the next topic.

tasks.title: Print a greeting
tasks.brief: Print the exact text Hello, world!
hints: Text needs to go inside quotes for Python to treat it as text: print("...")
print("Hello, world!")

tasks.title: Two lines
tasks.brief: Print I love coding on the first line. Print Python is fun on the second line.
hints: You need two separate print() calls, one for each line.
print("I love coding"), then print("Python is fun")

tests.expect:
I love coding
Python is fun

tasks.title: Text then a number
tasks.brief: Print the word Score on one line. Print the number 100 on the next line.
hints: Score needs quotes because it's text. 100 doesn't, because it's a number.
print("Score"), then print(100)

tasks.title: Three lines
tasks.brief: Print three lines, in this exact order: Chocolate, then Football, then Music.
hints: Use three separate print() calls, one per line, in the order given.

print("Chocolate")
print("Football")
print("Music")

tasks.title: Robot introduction
tasks.brief:
Print exactly these three lines, using three separate print() calls:

A robot says:
Beep boop!
I am learning Python.
hints: Three print() calls, one per line, in the exact order and spelling given.

print("A robot says:")
print("Beep boop!")
print("I am learning Python.")

tests.expect:
A robot says:
Beep boop!
I am learning Python.

tasks.title: Echo it back
tasks.brief: Input some text from the user and print it straight back out, exactly as it was typed.
hints: You can pass input() straight into print() without storing it first.
print(input())

tasks.title: Store and show
tasks.brief: Input the user's favourite colour and store it under the name colour. Print colour.
hints: colour = input() stores the answer, then print(colour) shows it.

colour = input()
print(colour)

tasks.title: Two answers
tasks.brief: Input the user's first name and store it under first_name. Input their favourite food and store it under food. Print first_name, then print food, each on its own line.
hints: You need two separate input() calls, one stored in each name.

first_name = input()
food = input()
print(first_name)
print(food)

tasks.title: Say it twice
tasks.brief: Input a word from the user. Print it, then print it again on the next line.
hints: Store the input under a name first, then you can print that name twice.

word = input()
print(word)
print(word)

tasks.title: Swap the order
tasks.brief: Input two words, one at a time. Print the second word first, then the first word, each on its own line.
hints: Store both answers under two different names before printing anything.

first = input()
second = input()
print(second)
print(first)

tasks.title: Join two words
tasks.brief: Print the result of joining the text Sun and the text Flower together with +, so it reads SunFlower.
hints: + glues two strings together with nothing extra added.
print("Sun" + "Flower")

tasks.title: Add a space
tasks.brief: Print the text Good and the text Morning joined with +, with a space between them, so it reads Good Morning.
hints: + doesn't add spaces on its own — join in a separate " " piece in between.
print("Good" + " " + "Morning")

tasks.title: Greet the user
tasks.brief: Input the user's name. Print Hello, followed by their name, joined with +, so entering Ada prints Hello, Ada. Remember + doesn't add spaces or punctuation for you.
hints: Build the greeting text so it already includes the comma and space: "Hello, ".

name = input()
print("Hello, " + name)

tasks.title: Build a sentence
tasks.brief: Input a person's name. Input their pet's name. Print a sentence in the format <name>'s pet is called <pet>, built using +. For example, entering Ada then Rex prints Ada's pet is called Rex.
hints: Break the sentence into pieces: name, then "'s pet is called ", then pet.

name = input()
pet = input()
print(name + "'s pet is called " + pet)

tasks.title: Three-part message
tasks.brief: Input a name, then input a place, then input an activity. Print a sentence in the format <name> went to <place> to <activity>, built entirely using +. For example, entering Ada, then the park, then play gives Ada went to the park to play.
hints: Break it into pieces: name, " went to ", place, " to ", activity.

name = input()
place = input()
activity = input()
print(name + " went to " + place + " to " + activity)

tests.expect: Ada went to the park to play
Sam went to school to learn
